title: Ψύλλα καὶ βοῦς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 358. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements, [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t:
Ψύλλα δέ ποτε τὸν βοῦν οὕτως ἠρώτα·
« Τί δὴ [παθὼν] ἀνθρώποις ὁσημέραι δουλεύεις,
καὶ ταῦτα ὑπερμεγέθης καὶ ἀνδρεῖος [τυγχάνων],
μοῦ σάρκας αὐτῶν οἰκτίστως διασπώσης
καὶ τὸ αἷμα ⟨αὐτῶν⟩ χανδόθεν πινούσης ; »
sentences.tr:
Psylla de pote ton boun houtōs ērōta·
« Ti dē [pathōn] anthrōpois hosēmerai douleueis,
kai tauta hypermegethēs kai andreios [tynchanōn],
mou sarkas autōn oiktistōs diaspōsēs
kai to haima ⟨autōn⟩ chandothen pinousēs ; »
sentences.l: And a flea once asked the ox thus: « Why then, [having suffered,] do you serve men day after day, and that [happening to be] enormous and brave, while I most piteously tear their flesh and drink ⟨their⟩ blood by the gulp? »
sentences.i: A flea once asked the ox: « Why on earth do you slave for men day after day, huge and brave as you are, when I tear their flesh most piteously and drink their blood by the gulp? »
sentences.n: τί … παθών, literally 'having suffered what', is an idiom of astonishment — 'what has got into you, that…'; with παθών bracketed away the question is left as a plain 'why?'. The two sets of brackets in this sentence pull opposite ways: [παθών] and [τυγχάνων] are words Chambry judges interpolated and deletes, ⟨αὐτῶν⟩ one he adds. καὶ ταῦτα, 'and that too', concedes a point against what has just been said. μοῦ … διασπώσης … πινούσης is a genitive absolute with the flea herself as its subject.

sentences.t:
Ὁ δ’· « Οὐκ ἄχαρίς εἰμι μερόπων γένει·
στέργομαι γὰρ παρὰ αὐτῶν καὶ φιλοῦμαι [ἐκτόπως],
τρίβομαί τε συχνῶς μέτωπόν [τε] καὶ ὤμους. »
sentences.tr:
Ho d’· « Ouk acharis eimi meropōn genei·
stergomai gar para autōn kai philoumai [ektopōs],
tribomai te sychnōs metōpon [te] kai ōmous. »
sentences.l: And he: « I am not ungrateful to the race of mortals; for I am loved by them and cherished [beyond measure], and I am rubbed often on forehead and shoulders. »
sentences.i: And the ox said: « I owe the race of mortals no ingratitude; they love me and are fond of me, and they rub my forehead and shoulders often. »
sentences.n: Ὁ δέ with no verb of speaking at all — ἔφη is simply left out and the reply follows, as it constantly does in this collection. μέροπες, 'mortal men', is an epic word, part of the raised diction these late flea pieces reach for. τρίβομαι μέτωπον καὶ ὤμους keeps an accusative of the part affected beside the passive verb. [ἐκτόπως] and [τε] are Chambry's deletions; the particle has no English realisation and so leaves no trace in the literal line.

sentences.t:
Ἡ δέ· « Ἀλλ’ ἐμοὶ γοῦν τέως τῇ δειλαίᾳ
ἡ σοὶ φίλη τρίψις οἴκτιστος ⟨δὴ⟩ μόρος,
ὅτε καὶ τύχῃ συμβαίνει ⟨μοι ἁλῶναι⟩. »
sentences.tr:
Hē de· « All’ emoi goun teōs tēi deilaiāi
hē soi philē tripsis oiktistos ⟨dē⟩ moros,
hote kai tychēi symbainei ⟨moi halōnai⟩. »
sentences.l: And she: « But for me at any rate, meanwhile, wretch that I am, that rubbing which is dear to you is ⟨indeed⟩ a most piteous death, when indeed by chance it comes about ⟨that I am caught⟩. »
sentences.i: And the flea said: « But for me, poor wretch, the rubbing you are so fond of is meanwhile a most piteous death, whenever by chance I am caught in it. »
sentences.n: ἐμοὶ … τῇ δειλαίᾳ sets the adjective in apposition to the pronoun, 'for me, the wretched one'. τέως is 'meanwhile, as things stand up to now'. ἡ σοὶ φίλη τρίψις wraps a dative inside the article and its noun — a shape Greek does easily and English cannot. τύχῃ is a dative of manner, 'by chance'. Chambry supplies ⟨δή⟩ and ⟨μοι ἁλῶναι⟩; without the latter συμβαίνει has no subject.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οἱ διὰ τοῦ λόγου ἀλαζόνες καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ εὐτελοῦς ἡττῶνται.
sentences.tr: Hoti hoi dia tou logou alazones kai hypo tou eutelous hēttōntai.
sentences.l: That braggarts in speech are worsted even by what is of no account.
sentences.i: The story shows that braggarts in speech are worsted even by what is of no account.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἀλαζών is the braggart impostor of Greek comedy, the man whose claims outrun him. καί here is 'even', and τοῦ εὐτελοῦς is a neuter adjective used as a noun — 'the cheap thing', the flea. One printing note, on the last line of the book: the scanned page shows a blank of exactly one letter-width where the eta of ἡττῶνται belongs — the line begins 6.7 pt right of the page's prose margin, and the missing slot measures about 7 pt, the width of a single η. The word is given whole here, since no other reading is possible; this is the one place in the fable where the text is not the ink.
